implementation_notes: C++11 composes the pattern from the standard library: the producer pushes a reserved value (or a tagged std::variant/optional) onto a std::queue protected by std::mutex and signals std::condition_variable, while the consumer waits with cv.wait(lock, [&]{ return !q.empty(); }) before checking for the sentinel. One reserved value is posted per consumer; the wait predicate covers spurious wake-ups. On C++20 the sentinel can be dropped entirely - std::jthread supplies a std::stop_token and condition_variable_any::wait(lock, stop_token, pred) wakes on request_stop() - so no value has to share the data plane (see the jthread-stop-token variant).
pitfalls: A reserved T value collides when T can legitimately carry it (a default-constructed Job); use std::optional, a variant or an explicit tag instead.
One sentinel stops one consumer: pushing N pills for N threads (or a shared done flag plus notify_all) is the injector's contract.
Dropping the wait predicate makes the consumer wake on spurious notifications and observe an empty queue.
A std::thread left joinable - or one still waiting for a pill that never comes - terminates the process; prefer std::jthread, whose destructor requests stop and joins.

variants.name: std::jthread + std::stop_token cooperative stop (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 replaces the in-band sentinel with cooperative cancellation state: the worker runs as a std::jthread, waits with condition_variable_any::wait(lock, stop_token, pred) (which wakes when stop is requested or work is available), and exits once stop is requested and the queue is drained; the jthread destructor requests stop and joins, so no value shares the data plane and no per-consumer pill bookkeeping is needed. Choose it when the whole toolchain is C++20 and the stop signal should not be confusable with payloads; keep the sentinel when consumers are plain std::threads, non-C++20 targets, or when the stop must travel through the queue itself (for example to a consumer in another component).
pitfalls: The stop_token overloads live on std::condition_variable_any, not std::condition_variable - the latter does not compile with a stop token.
request_stop() alone wakes a waiting worker only through the stop callback that condition_variable_any::wait registers; plain wait() needs an extra notify_all().
The jthread destructor requests stop and joins, so a worker that ignores stop blocks the destructor; the loop must return on stop once drained.
